title: The Science, and Culture, of Reading Instruction
author: Aldeman, Chad
summary: Chad Aldeman analyzes a Fordham Institute survey of 1,244 K-3 teachers that reveals both genuine progress and persistent failures in the science of reading movement: 40+ states have enacted SOR laws and LETRS-trained teachers demonstrably know and teach better, but four serious challenges remain. First, teacher preparation programs are still failing: teachers who relied most on their preservice college training scored lower on reading knowledge quizzes than those who relied on any other source -- including on-the-job learning -- meaning colleges are actively undermining the reform. Second, high-poverty schools show a larger phonics-commitment gap (43% of teachers ambivalent about phonics vs. 25% in affluent schools), meaning the students most dependent on school-delivered instruction are the least likely to receive it correctly. Third, 58% of teachers still hold an incorrect mental model of reading comprehension -- believing it is a transferable set of generic skills rather than a function of topic-specific knowledge and vocabulary -- which drives instruction away from content-rich curricula toward strategy drilling with no transfer effect. Fourth, cultural resistance is real: professional identity, pedagogical habit, and genuine belief in balanced literacy make teachers resistant to reimagining their practice, and the SOR movement's momentum is fragile enough that declaring victory prematurely could waste a rare window of reform.
points: Teacher preparation programs are the single largest bottleneck in reading reform: the more a teacher relied on preservice training, the less they knew about evidence-based reading instruction -- colleges are not just neutral but actively counterproductive.

High-poverty schools have the largest phonics-commitment gap (43% ambivalent vs. 25% in affluent schools), meaning the students most dependent on school instruction are the least likely to receive it correctly -- an equity crisis inside a reform movement.

The majority of teachers (58%) hold an incorrect mental model of reading comprehension: they believe it is a transferable generic skill rather than a function of prior knowledge and vocabulary, which drives instruction toward strategy drilling that has little transfer effect.

History, science, and the arts are not curricular luxuries but the cognitive raw material that makes reading comprehension possible -- cutting content subjects when reading scores are low is precisely backwards.

Cultural change in reading instruction is real but fragile: professional identity and pedagogical habit are deeply ingrained, and the worst outcome would be to declare victory prematurely before beliefs and practices have fully shifted.
quotes: The more a teacher relied on what they learned in their teacher preparation program, the less they knew about evidence-based reading instruction.

Only 2 percent of teachers said their preservice program was where they learned the most about effective reading practices. In contrast, 33 percent said they learned the most on the job, and 21 percent credited in-service professional development.

Teachers in high-poverty schools are, on average, less informed about and committed to reading science than their colleagues in more affluent settings... Children who come from under-resourced homes depend on their teachers more than children who have compensating resources at home.

When teachers were asked to choose between two statements about reading comprehension, 58 percent chose the wrong one. They believed that reading comprehension is 'a set of generalizable skills (like finding the main idea and making inferences) that can be applied to most texts.'

These generic comprehension strategies have very little transferable effect. What actually drives comprehension is knowledge. A child who knows a lot about the American Revolution will understand a passage about Paul Revere far better than a child who was drilled in comprehension 'strategies' but who knows nothing about history.
This is why history, science, and the arts aren't luxuries to be cut when reading scores are low -- they're the very substance that makes reading comprehension possible.

Teachers who spent years building expertise in one approach, and who genuinely believed they were helping children, are being asked to fundamentally reimagine what good reading instruction looks like. That's not easy. Professional identity is real, and pedagogical habits are deeply ingrained.
